attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, published under his name.

semantics.note: Faithful to the statement. The slight softener 'don't really have' is dropped, but the meaning is the same. This is a present-tense observation about the state of the field.

contract.note: Marcus gave no threshold for 'adequate'. The contract's reading (a repeatable integration method with manageable regressions) fits his whack-a-mole context and is an ordinary reading. The Jan-May 2022 window was chosen by the evaluator but is reasonable.

evidence.note: ICSE 2022 industry study, May 2022, inside the window. It reports component entanglement and performance regressions in ML testing. This fits Marcus's concern, but it is one survey and does not show that no methodology was adequate.
Gato preprint, May 2022. It shows multi-task integration but says nothing about dependable modification or regression control, so it does not meet the contradiction condition.
2017 Google rubric of ML tests. It predates the window and shows that engineering practices existed, but not that they were adequate for complex cognitive systems.

reviews.rationale: e1 partly supports Marcus's concern, and nothing in the packet shows a proven, repeatable integration method by May 2022. But the support condition needs broad evidence across applications, and the packet has one industry survey and admits there is no adequacy threshold or comprehensive comparison. The evidence does not settle the field-wide claim either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his own post. Co-authorship with Davis is mentioned, but Marcus endorses it.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'will not' makes this a scored forecast. The 2029 horizon, the 10,000-line threshold, the 'reliably' and 'bug-free' requirements, both input routes and the library exclusion are all kept.

contract.note: Reading 'in 2029' as the whole year, and 'reliably' and 'bug-free' as repeatable, independently checked correctness, is an ordinary reading. The early-contradiction rule is strict but fair.

evidence.note: Anthropic's Feb 2026 report on a 100k-line compiler, a company disclosure. The same report describes defects, regressions and heavy expert work on testing, so it does not meet the bug-free, reliable or non-expert criteria. Early resolution is not triggered.

Anthropic's Oct 2026 report, a company disclosure. It covers proofs about existing software and says itself that verified does not mean bug-free. It does not show qualifying new programs built from natural-language specs.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is 2029-12-31, after the evaluation date. Neither item meets the early-contradiction rule: the compiler had acknowledged bugs and regressions and relied on expert test design, and the verification work concerns existing code. Failures before 2029 cannot support the forecast, so it stays unscored until the horizon passes.

attribution.note: The statement is about Musk's predictions, but the description of his track record is Marcus's own factual claim in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 2015 two-year attribution, the 'pretty much every year since' qualifier and the claim of non-arrival.

contract.note: The context is Musk's own track record, so scoping 'it still hasn't happened' to Tesla is the ordinary reading. Treating 'pretty much the same' as repeated near-term forecasts is fair to the qualifier. Waymo is properly treated as context only.

evidence.note: Fortune, Dec 2015: Musk predicts complete autonomy in about two years. This confirms the 2015 attribution.
Inverse, Apr 2019: robotaxi forecast for 2020, plus a dated chronology of earlier yearly forecasts.
BBC, Jul 2020: Musk predicts complete autonomy by year end, and notes Tesla was then at Level 2.
Ars Technica, May 2021: Level 5 predicted for end of 2021, Musk's 2016 'solved problem' remark, and Tesla's own engineer telling regulators it was Level 2.
CNBC, Feb 2022: ride-alongs show FSD still needing supervision and suffering glitches, and the article reports Musk's renewed 2022 forecast.
Waymo disclosure, Oct 2020: driverless service at another company in a limited area. It matters only under an industry-wide reading the context does not support.

reviews.rationale: Dated reports confirm the 2015 two-year prediction and near-term autonomy forecasts in 2016-2022, which satisfies 'pretty much every year'. As of early 2022, Tesla still relied on supervised driving. Waymo's limited driverless service does not undercut a Tesla-scoped reading.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps Marcus's reasons (every home differs and has its own safety risks; roads are engineered alike) and correctly does not treat Optimus as a confirmed domestic robot. 'I can promise you' is firm, not hedged.

contract.note: Reading the claim as 'substantially broader adaptable cognition' is ordinary. The Jan-May 2022 window is somewhat artificial for a timeless comparison, but it is harmless. 'Way beyond' has no magnitude, so the result turns on the evaluator's reading.

evidence.note: BEHAVIOR benchmark, Aug 2021, before the window. It documents the breadth of household tasks but makes no comparison with driving.
SayCan, Apr 2022. It shows progress on real kitchen tasks and names limits in skill range, but does not measure required intelligence against driving.
Waymo disclosure, May 2022. It says driving fundamentals are largely the same everywhere but also stresses the long tail of rare events. It is not a comparative requirements analysis.

reviews.rationale: The contract needs comparative task analyses showing that domestic work requires substantially broader cognition than driving. The packet admits no such comparison was found. The items show breadth on both sides but do not settle the comparison or the 'way beyond' magnitude.
